exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 17–22, all vectors and subspaces are in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$W$$ , then multiplying $$\mathbf{v}_{3}$$ by a scalar $$c$$ gives a new orthogonal basis $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} c\mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ .

(T/F) If $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \textbf{x}_{1} \text{,} \textbf{x}_{2} \text{,} \textbf{x}_{3} \right\}$$ with $$\left\{ \textbf{x}_{1} \text{,} \textbf{x}_{2} \text{,} \textbf{x}_{3} \right\}$$ linearly independent, and if $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal set in $$W$$ , then $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ is a basis for $$W$$ .

(T/F) The Gram–Schmidt process produces from a linearly independent set $$\left\{ \textbf{x}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \textbf{x}_{p} \right\}$$ an orthogonal set $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \right\}$$ with the property that for each $$k$$ , the vectors $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{k}$$ span the same subspace as that spanned by $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ .
(T/F) If $$\textbf{x}$$ is not in a subspace $$W$$ , then $$\textbf{x} - \text{proj} _{W}\textbf{x}$$ is not zero.
(T/F) If $$A = QR$$ , where $$Q$$ has orthonormal columns, then $$R = Q^{T}A$$ .
(T/F) In a QR factorization, say $$A = QR$$ (when $$A$$ has linearly independent columns), the columns of $$Q$$ form an orthonormal basis for the column space of $$A$$ .

Suppose $$A = Q R$$ , where $$Q$$ is $$m \times n$$ and $$R$$ is $$n \times n$$ . Show that if the columns of $$A$$ are linearly independent, then $$R$$ must be invertible. [Hint: Study the equation $$R\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ and use the fact that $$A = Q R$$ .]

Suppose $$A = Q R$$ , where $$R$$ is an invertible matrix. Show that $$A$$ and $$Q$$ have the same column space. [Hint: Given $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\text{Col} A$$ , show that $$\textbf{y} = Q\textbf{x}$$ for some $$\textbf{x}$$ . Also, given $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\text{Col} Q$$ , show that $$\textbf{y} = A\textbf{x}$$ for some $$\textbf{x}$$ .]

Suppose $$Q$$ is an $$n \times k$$ matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis for the subspace $$W_{k}$$ spanned by the first $$k$$ columns of $$A$$ . Then for $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , $$QQ^{T}\textbf{x}$$ is the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{x}$$ onto $$W_{k}$$ (Theorem 10 in Section 6.3). problem.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \textbf{x}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \textbf{x}_{2} - \frac{\textbf{x}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{1}}{\mathbf{v}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{1}}\mathbf{v}_{1} = \textbf{x}_{2} - 0\mathbf{v}_{1} = \textbf{x}_{2}$$ . So $$\left\{ \textbf{x}_{1} \text{,} \textbf{x}_{2} \right\}$$ is already orthogonal. All that is needed is to normalize the vectors. Let $$\textbf{u}_{1 } = \frac{1}{\parallel \textbf{v}_{1} \parallel} \textbf{v}_{1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / \sqrt{3} \\ 1 / \sqrt{3} \\ 1 / \sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix}$$

Instead of normalizing $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ directly, normalize $$\mathbf{v}_{2}^{\prime} = 3\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ instead: $$\textbf{u}_{2 } = \frac{1}{\parallel \mathbf{v}_{2}^{′} \parallel} \mathbf{v}_{2}^{′} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2} + \left(\left(\right. - 2 \left.\right)\right)^{2}}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / \sqrt{6} \\ 1 / \sqrt{6} \\ - 2 / \sqrt{6} \end{bmatrix}$$
Then $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ is an orthonormal basis for $$W$$ .

Since the columns of $$A$$ are linearly dependent, there is a nontrivial vector $$\textbf{x}$$ such that $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ . But then $$QR\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ . Applying Theorem 7 from Section 6.2 results in $$\text{∥} R\textbf{x} \text{∥} = \text{∥} QR\textbf{x} \text{∥} = \text{∥} \textbf{0} \text{∥} = 0$$ . But $$\text{∥} R\textbf{x} \text{∥} = 0$$ implies $$R\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ , by Theorem 1 from Section 6.1. Thus there is a nontrivial vector $$\textbf{x}$$ such that $$R\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ and hence, by the Invertible Matrix Theorem, $$R$$ cannot be invertible.
